segments.expected: "I meant your crossing." Dray's voice was perfectly flat. "Not your Ember. Anybody can beat an Ember on one door with an edge. I meant the thing you do that nobody else does, read off a mast, with your captain saying the count out loud so that I'd know the second it came. I've had that in my head since the ninth month." She looked down at her left leg, straight on the floor in its boot, and back up. "That's what I came two hundred miles on this for."

segments.expected: Kiva felt the head of the Commodore go. It did not go fast. Twenty-Eight's still door leaned from the floor, as Lyle had leaned, as everybody on the coast seemed to have learned in a week, and the head poles came out of the crooks of her elbows a finger at a time, because her forearms were not hands and could not close. Pru had the foot on her arms. Twenty-Eight's Hold put her wall across the litter's middle, between Pru and the head, and leaned it on nobody, and held it there. Marten took the foot poles from under Pru's crossed forearms with his own two good hands, gently, as a man takes a tray from a child.

segments.expected: Kiva could see what a crossing would do. She could see it as plainly as she had ever seen anything. Her hand door, the ward, low and flat at her hip, a wall between her and Dray's edge; then the count, one, two, three, and the gap, a quarter of a count with nothing open; and then her Ember, glad, and the low bound back with the head on her forearms, two paces, three, out of Dray's reach and across the chalk into Seven's half before Dray could come round to her left. It was her own certified crossing, hand to Ember. She had made it six times on two masts. She could feel exactly how it would go.

segments.expected: Dray did not go round to her left. Kiva had thought she might, and had bounded to Dray's left on purpose, toward the turn she did not like. Dray did not take the turn. She stepped across instead, with her right foot, the long way, and it was a count and a half and Kiva was a pace and a half off with a hundredweight on her arms and nothing open but the Ember, and that was not enough. Dray's edge came down flat on her back between the shoulder blades, quite lightly, as lightly as a woman puts her hand on a child's head.
